lesson.title: Same Protein, Different Code: Why Some Mutations Go Unnoticed
lesson.summary: A silent mutation changes a codon's DNA sequence but not the amino acid it specifies, a direct consequence of the genetic code's redundancy.
lesson.body:
Not every point mutation changes the protein it helps encode. The genetic code is degenerate, meaning most amino acids are specified by more than one codon: of the 61 codons that code for amino acids, many amino acids are represented by two, four, or even six different codons, and those synonymous codons for the same amino acid usually differ only at the third position of the triplet. Serine, for example, is coded for by UCU, UCC, UCA, UCG, AGU, and AGC. Because of this redundancy, a substitution that changes a codon into a different codon for the same amino acid produces no change at all in the resulting protein. This is called a silent mutation.

The earlier example of the codon UCA shows this directly. Changing its third base from A to G converts UCA into UCG. Both UCA and UCG code for serine, so the protein made from that gene is completely unchanged, even though the underlying DNA and mRNA sequence is not. The cell has no way to tell, from the protein alone, that anything happened at all.

This third position tolerance is sometimes called wobble, because the pairing between a codon's third base and the corresponding first base of the anticodon on transfer RNA is looser than pairing at the first two codon positions, allowing a single tRNA to recognize more than one codon. Since most synonymous substitutions fall at this third position, point mutations there are disproportionately likely to be silent compared to changes at the first or second position of a codon, where nearly every possible substitution changes the amino acid.

Silent does not always mean entirely without consequence, even though the protein's amino acid sequence stays the same. A synonymous codon can still be translated at a different speed if the cell has more or less of the matching tRNA available, and unusually slow or fast translation at a particular codon can occasionally affect how a protein folds as it is made. A synonymous change that happens to fall near an intron boundary can, in rare cases, disrupt a sequence that the splicing machinery uses to recognize that boundary. These effects are the exception rather than the rule, but they are a reminder that silent describes the protein sequence, not necessarily everything the mutation touches.
